title: Solitude in the crowd
hook: Naqshbandi Sufis keep a silent remembrance going while living ordinary lives

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was al-Ghazali's crisis: a doubt argument couldn't cure, and a way through by tasting. Your line was lost, then found.

A market at noon. Carts, voices, prices called across the stalls, someone haggling over a roll of cloth. In the middle of it a merchant is doing ordinary business: weighing, counting, smiling at a regular customer. And inside, silently, without a word on his lips, he is remembering God. Nobody around him can tell. That scene is the picture behind a short Persian phrase that Naqshbandi Sufis keep close: khalwat dar anjuman. Solitude in the crowd.
screen: `A MARKET AT NOON.` → `SILENT, INSIDE.` → `KHALWAT DAR ANJUMAN.`

segments.voice: The Naqshbandi order is one of the Sufi paths, named for Baha al-Din Naqshband. Its teachers kept a handful of short Persian phrases as signposts, and solitude in the crowd is one of them: outwardly with people, inwardly with God. A saying handed down in the order puts it even more simply: the hand at work, the heart with the Friend. You met dhikr, remembrance, on day two hundred sixty-nine. The Naqshbandi way puts its weight on the silent kind, dhikr of the heart, rather than remembrance said aloud. So a Naqshbandi can trade, cook, raise children, ride a crowded train, and keep the remembrance running underneath, unheard. Beside this phrase the order keeps others just as short. Awareness in the breath. Watch your step, eyes on where your feet are going. A journey inside your own homeland. Together they describe a path that doesn't need a cave. The Qur'an gives a picture of it, in Pickthall's translation: "Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah." The merchandise is still there. So is the sale. What changes is whether it pulls the heart away. Other Sufis go off into retreat, away from everyone, and tomorrow is about that. The Naqshbandi phrase doesn't throw retreat out. It carries it into the street.
screen: `OUTWARDLY WITH PEOPLE, INWARDLY WITH GOD.` · `THE HAND AT WORK, THE HEART WITH THE FRIEND.` · `REMEMBRANCE IN SILENCE.` · `RETREAT CARRIED INTO THE STREET.` · then, large: `NEITHER MERCHANDISE NOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Listen for the sounds of other people, voices, traffic, a door down the hall, a television somewhere, and don't shut them out; let them be the market around you. Underneath, keep one quiet thing going: if you pray, a silent word of remembrance carried on the breath, and if you don't, simply the breath itself, noticed in and out.
Solitude in the crowd. In Persian, khalwat dar anjuman: a Naqshbandi Sufi phrase for silent remembrance kept up in the middle of ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: alone in the crowd. The solitude is real; it just doesn't need an empty room. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Naqshbandi Sufis are taught a silent remembrance of the heart, kept up through work and family life, guided by short Persian principles such as solitude in the crowd and awareness in the breath.

chat.says: Do Sufis have to leave the world behind to stay close to God?
options: The Naqshbandi phrase says no: outwardly with people, inwardly with God, even at work.
Yes; remembrance only counts when it's done far from people and noise.
No; Naqshbandis say retreat is wrong, so they never go away at all.
chat.meaning: Khalwat dar anjuman, solitude in the crowd: the hand at work, the heart with the Friend. The Naqshbandi way carries retreat into the street.

notes: Confirm Pickthall wording of 24:37: 'Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah'.

The Naqshbandi principles are often listed as a set (traditionally attributed in part to Abd al-Khaliq Ghujduvani, with additions by Baha al-Din Naqshband); the script gives no count and no attribution beyond 'its teachers'. Confirm.
'The hand at work, the heart with the Friend' (dast ba kar, dil ba yar) is described as 'a saying handed down in the order'; it is commonly attributed to Baha al-Din Naqshband. Confirm.
'The Naqshbandi way puts its weight on silent remembrance' (dhikr khafi): confirm phrasing; some Naqshbandi branches also practice vocal dhikr.
The market scene in the hook is an illustration, not a sourced story.
